passage:
The prices dropped the week Ritu's scooter needed a new part, and the bank's message about the monthly instalment arrived on the same morning. Hrithik, a colleague at the next desk, looked over. "Stop it for now. Wait till the bottom, then buy."
Ritu opened her notebook. On the first page, written before any fall: "Same amount, same date, every month. No guessing."
"I can't tell where the bottom is," Ritu said. "Nobody can. But if the price is low, the same money buys more units."
"And the scooter?"
"I'll cut something else for a month."
The instalment went through at ten, and Ritu turned back to work with her stomach still tight.

qa.q: What did Ritu's notebook say on its first page?
qa.a: The notebook said "Same amount, same date, every month. No guessing."

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling as the instalment went through?
qa.a: Ritu felt nervous, as the tight stomach shows, but she stuck to the rule she had set.

qa.q: What could Ritu do if money ever feels too tight to keep the instalment?
qa.a: Rather than changing the rule in a worried moment, Ritu could talk it through with a qualified adviser first and decide calmly.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have seen Ritu's choice?
qa.a: Hrithik probably thought it risky and wanted to protect Ritu from more losses, which is why Hrithik said to stop it for now.

grounding: The passage shows an investor keeping a fixed monthly instalment through a fall, on a rule made beforehand, buying more units at lower prices without guessing the bottom.

passage:
When Mohit started his monthly investment plan at twenty-three, he wrote a note to himself in his phone: "Rule: the SIP runs every month, whatever the news. Stop only if I lose my job or need the money." His uncle Jagdish, who had invested for decades, had suggested writing it down "for the day you'll want to stop".
That day came in November. The market fell sharply. His office in Gurugram buzzed with talk of selling. Mohit's thumb hovered over "Pause SIP".
Then he opened the note. He still had his job. He didn't need the money for years. So he left it running.
Each month the same instalment bought more units, because prices were lower. He didn't know if it was the bottom and didn't try to guess. A year later, when he checked, those cheap months had become the best part of his returns. He called Jagdish Chachu to tell him.

qa.a: "Rule: the SIP runs every month, whatever the news. Stop only if I lose my job or need the money."

qa.q: How did Mohit feel when his thumb hovered over "Pause SIP"?
qa.a: Mohit felt tempted and anxious, pulled by the office talk of selling.

qa.q: Why did writing the rule in advance help?
qa.a: It let Mohit decide calmly before the fall, so on the frightening day he could follow his earlier thinking instead of the mood around him.

qa.q: How might Jagdish Chachu feel when Mohit calls?
qa.a: Jagdish Chachu is likely pleased and proud that the advice to write it down helped on the hard day.

grounding: It shows a young investor keeping a fixed monthly instalment going through a fall, following a rule set beforehand and buying more units without guessing the bottom.

passage:
"Chandrika, have you stopped your SIP? Everyone in my office has," Himani said, dropping into the chair.
"No. It went out on the fifth, like every month."
"But the market is down so much!"
"That's the point. Same amount, lower price. I get more units this month than last."
"What if it keeps falling?"
"Then next month I get even more. I'm not trying to guess the bottom. I can't."
"How are you so calm?"
Chandrika pulled out her phone and showed a note. "I wrote this when I started, two years ago: 'Keep the SIP going through falls. Only stop if I lose my income or need the money soon.' I still have my job, and this money is for when I'm fifty."
"So you just follow your own note?"
"Past me was calmer than present me. I trust her."
Himani laughed. "Maybe I should talk to someone before I stop mine."
"That's the first sensible thing you've said today."

qa.q: When does Chandrika's SIP go out?
qa.a: On the fifth, like every month.

qa.q: Why is Chandrika calm while others stop their SIPs?
qa.a: Chandrika feels calm because a rule was made two years ago for exactly this moment, and the money is meant for age fifty.

qa.q: What does Himani decide, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To talk to someone before stopping, rather than copying what her office is doing in a panic.

qa.q: How does Himani see the market fall at first?
qa.a: Himani is alarmed, worried because everyone in the office has stopped their SIPs.

grounding: It shows a young investor continuing a fixed monthly SIP through a fall, following a rule set in calmer times and buying more units without guessing the bottom.
